prompt: Write an email to a colleague about pests eating the vegetables. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the email only.
final_message:
Subject: The vegetable situation

Dear Martin,

I write with news of the garden, none of it good. Something has been eating my vegetables, and I have lately come to suspect that it is several somethings, working in shifts.

The first offender is the cabbage worm, a pale green creature of modest size and immodest appetite. It has reduced my broccoli to a sort of lace, which would be admirable in a tablecloth but is of limited use at dinner. The second is a slug, or possibly a regiment of them. I never see them at work; I see only the silver trails in the morning, like the marks left by a tiny and very dull army. The third, and I fear the worst, is whatever has been at the zucchini. Every other year I have had more zucchini than any household could decently use, and was reduced to leaving them on neighbors' porches under cover of darkness. This year I have had two. I do not know who is responsible, but I suspect the squash bug, and I intend to treat the matter with the gravity of a court of inquiry.

I have tried the usual remedies. I picked the worms off by hand, one at a time, which took the better part of a Saturday and taught me more about the underside of a cabbage leaf than any man needs to know. I set out saucers of beer for the slugs; they came, they drank, and I am told they died happy, which is more than I can say for the broccoli. My wife has suggested that I net the whole bed. I have pointed out that this would make the garden look like a fishing operation, and she has pointed out that a fishing operation would at least catch something.

Since you have kept a garden longer than I have, and with better results, I would value your advice. Do you have any trusted method for the squash bug? I have read that one may lay a board on the ground at night and collect the bugs beneath it in the morning; this sounds either very clever or very foolish, and I cannot yet tell which. I have also heard that marigolds keep off all manner of pests, though the marigolds I planted last spring were eaten before they could discourage anyone.

If you are free next week, come and look at the patch yourself. I will provide tea, and you may provide a second opinion; it is a fair exchange. Bring a hat, as the sun is still strong in the afternoon, and a stout pair of shoes, as the slugs are not particular about where they leave their calling cards.

Yours in the matter of the cabbage,

Walter
